content: Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS), which occurs due to opioid withdrawal in newborns, can lead to significant complications such as disruption of the mother-infant bond, abnormal sleep-wake cycles, feeding difficulties, weight loss, seizures, and long-term neurodevelopmental issues. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of sedatives compared to control treatments (placebo, standard care, or non-pharmacological interventions) in managing NAS caused by opioid withdrawal. Additionally, the review aimed to identify which sedative is the most effective and safe for this condition. A systematic search was conducted on September 17, 2020, using CENTRAL and MEDLINE databases, as well as clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized trials, and cluster-randomized trials that enrolled infants with NAS born to mothers with opioid dependence. Only studies with at least 80% follow-up were included. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by three reviewers, and the GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. The review included 10 trials involving 581 infants with NAS secondary to maternal opioid use during pregnancy. The studies compared various sedatives and treatment regimens. However, the data available for sensitivity analysis were limited, particularly for studies with a low risk of bias. 1. Phenobarbital vs. Supportive Care Alone: One study suggested that there may be little or no difference in treatment failure between phenobarbital combined with supportive care and supportive care alone (risk ratio [RR] 2.73, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.94 to 7.94; 62 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No infants experienced clinical seizures in this comparison. The study did not report outcomes such as mortality, neurodevelopmental disability, or adverse events. Phenobarbital use may increase the duration of hospitalization (mean difference [MD] 20.80 days, 95% CI 13.64 to 27.96) and treatment duration (MD 17.90 days, 95% CI 11.98 to 23.82) compared to supportive care alone (62 participants; very low-certainty evidence). 2. Phenobarbital vs. Diazepam: Phenobarbital may reduce treatment failure compared to diazepam (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.62; 139 participants; 2 studies; low-certainty evidence). Mortality, neurodevelopmental disability, and adverse events were not reported in these studies. One study indicated there may be little or no difference in hospitalization duration (MD 3.89 days, 95% CI -1.20 to 8.98) or treatment duration (MD 4.30 days, 95% CI -0.73 to 9.33) between the two groups (32 participants; low-certainty evidence). 3. Phenobarbital vs. Chlorpromazine: Phenobarbital may reduce treatment failure compared to chlorpromazine (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.92; 138 participants; 2 studies; very low-certainty evidence). No infants experienced seizures in this comparison. Mortality and neurodevelopmental disability were not reported. One study suggested there may be little or no difference in hospitalization duration (MD 7.00 days, 95% CI -3.51 to 17.51; 87 participants; low-certainty evidence). No adverse events were reported in 100 infants studied. 4. Phenobarbital and Opioid vs. Opioid Alone: One study reported no treatment failures or clinical seizures in either group (low-certainty evidence). Mortality, neurodevelopmental disability, and adverse events were not reported. Phenobarbital combined with an opioid may reduce hospitalization duration compared to opioid alone (MD -43.50 days, 95% CI -59.18 to -27.82; 20 participants; low-certainty evidence). 5. Clonidine and Opioid vs. Opioid Alone: One study suggested there may be little or no difference in treatment failure between clonidine combined with dilute tincture of opium (DTO) and DTO alone (RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.59; 80 participants; very low-certainty evidence). All five treatment failures occurred in the DTO group. There may be little or no difference in seizure occurrence (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.68; 80 participants; very low-certainty evidence). All three seizures occurred in the DTO group. Mortality after discharge may show little or no difference (RR 7.00, 95% CI 0.37 to 131.28; 80 participants; very low-certainty evidence). All three deaths occurred in the clonidine and DTO group. Neurodevelopmental disability was not reported. There may be little or no difference in treatment duration (MD -4.00 days, 95% CI -8.33 to 0.33; 80 participants; very low-certainty evidence). One adverse event occurred in the clonidine and DTO group. There may be little or no difference in rebound NAS after treatment cessation, although all seven cases occurred in the clonidine and DTO group. 6. Clonidine and Opioid vs. Phenobarbital and Opioid: There may be little or no difference in treatment failure between these two regimens (RR 2.27, 95% CI 0.98 to 5.25; 2 studies, 93 participants; very low-certainty evidence). One study reported one seizure in the clonidine and morphine group, with no mortalities in either group. Neurodevelopmental disability was not reported. Clonidine and opioid may increase hospitalization duration (MD 7.13 days, 95% CI 6.38 to 7.88) and treatment duration (MD 7.57 days, 95% CI 3.97 to 11.17) compared to phenobarbital and opioid (2 studies, 91 participants; low-certainty evidence). There may be little or no difference in adverse events (RR 1.55, 95% CI 0.44 to 5.40; 2 studies, 93 participants; very low-certainty evidence). However, oversedation occurred only in the phenobarbital and morphine group, while hypotension, rebound hypertension, and rebound NAS occurred only in the clonidine and morphine group. Conclusions: Phenobarbital may increase hospitalization and treatment duration but may reduce the time to regain birth weight and the duration of daily supportive care compared to supportive care alone (very low-certainty evidence). Phenobarbital may reduce treatment failure compared to diazepam (low-certainty evidence) and chlorpromazine (very low-certainty evidence). Clonidine combined with an opioid may increase hospitalization and treatment duration compared to phenobarbital combined with an opioid (low-certainty evidence). There is insufficient data to determine the safety and frequency of adverse events for infants treated with combinations of opioids and sedatives, including phenobarbital and clonidine.
